rubrics.rubric: Does the redesigned Level 1 instrument (Deliverable 3, Section 2) address specific weaknesses visible in the current survey data, including format-specific questions for virtual sessions that scored poorly?
criterion: The redesigned survey must include at least one format-specific question addressing virtual delivery challenges, given that virtual sessions scored significantly lower than in-person (Virtual 2.58/5 vs. In-Person 3.00/5 across 338 responses).
Common open feedback themes from the current survey data (e.g., outdated materials, excessive slide reading, poor scheduling) should inform new question items in the redesigned instrument.

The instrument must incorporate at least one retrospective pre/post knowledge self-assessment item modeled on the NC State Tool-1A format from the Kirkpatrick reference PDF, using a before/after knowledge rating matrix on a 5-point scale.

rubrics.rubric: Does the Levels 2-4 Plan (Deliverable 3, Section 3) include pre/post knowledge assessments with 8-10 items each for the two highest composite-risk courses, with items that test specific OSHA-standard knowledge rather than generic safety awareness?
criterion: The two highest composite-risk courses selected for assessment must be chosen from among PPE-101, FIRE-101, HAZ-101, or FORK-201, which have the most training-related incidents (5, 5, 5, and 4 respectively).
Each of the two selected courses must have pre/post assessments containing 8-10 items each.

Assessment items must test specific, verifiable knowledge points aligned with OSHA standards (e.g., for LOTO: energy control procedures under 29 CFR 1910.147; for HazCom: SDS reading and GHS labeling under 29 CFR 1910.1200; for PPE: selection criteria and inspection procedures under 29 CFR 1910.132).
Generic questions like 'Did you learn something new?' are insufficient — items must reference specific regulatory content or procedural knowledge.

rubrics.rubric: Does the Levels 2-4 Plan include a 90-day supervisor observation checklist with specific observable behaviors tied to OSHA standards for the two highest-risk courses?
criterion: The 90-day supervisor observation checklist must contain specific, observable behavioral indicators rather than vague criteria (e.g., for PPE under 29 CFR 1910.132: selects correct PPE for the specific hazard, inspects PPE before each use, properly dons/doffs PPE, stores PPE correctly).

If LOTO is a target course, observable behaviors must include: identifies all energy sources before servicing, applies lockout/tagout devices in proper sequence, verifies zero energy state before work begins, removes devices only after all employees are clear.
The checklist must reference the specific OSHA standard subsections that define the required behaviors, connecting training content to on-the-job performance (Kirkpatrick Level 3 — Behavior).

rubrics.rubric: Does the Training Plan include at least one session per month for every OSHA-required course that had a training-related incident in the past 12 months?
criterion: The six courses with training-related incidents must be identified: PPE-101 (5 incidents), FIRE-101 (5 incidents), HAZ-101 (5 incidents), FORK-201 (4 incidents), ELEC-201 (3 incidents), and LOTO-201 (2 incidents).
Each of these six courses must appear at least once per calendar month within the 13-week Q2 schedule (April, May, June/early July), meaning a minimum of 3 sessions per course across the quarter.
The monthly scheduling of each course must be verifiable from the actual schedule, not just stated as a principle or guideline.

rubrics.rubric: Does the ROI projection (Deliverable 3, Section 4) use actual baseline metrics from the incident log and cost data from Deliverable 2, rather than hypothetical numbers, to project expected savings from reduced incidents versus the $38,000 investment?
criterion: The ROI calculation must use actual baseline data from the incident log: 52 incidents over roughly 14 months, 23 OSHA recordable incidents, and 129 total lost work days.

The ROI projection must estimate cost of incidents using actual lost work days and OSHA recordable counts, with industry benchmarks for direct/indirect costs (typically $40,000–$60,000+ per OSHA recordable incident).

The projection must compare the $38,000 training investment against the potential reduction in incident costs, using reasonable and stated assumptions about expected percentage reduction in incidents from improved training.
Baseline metrics (current incident rate, recordable rate, lost work days) must be explicitly stated and sourced from the provided data, with target values set for end of Q3 2025.

rubrics.rubric: Does the Compliance Matrix correctly use five status categories (Current, Expiring within 60 days, Overdue, Never Completed, Failed) and include the date of last completion for each employee-course combination across all nine OSHA-required courses?
criterion: The matrix must map all 45 unique employees against all 9 OSHA-required courses (Fire Prevention & Extinguisher Use, Confined Space Entry, Bloodborne Pathogens, Emergency Action Plan Review, Electrical Safety Awareness, Hazard Communication/HazCom, Lockout/Tagout/LOTO Procedures, PPE, Forklift Safety Certification).

Each cell must show one of the five specified statuses (Current, Expiring within 60 days, Overdue, Never Completed, Failed) and the date of last completion (or N/A for Never Completed), with 'Expiring within 60 days' calculated from Refresher_Due_Date relative to the assumed current date in early 2025.
The Compliance Matrix must document how the four source data statuses (Completed, Incomplete, Failed, Overdue) are mapped to the five task-specified matrix categories.

rubrics.rubric: Does the response correctly identify and highlight the 10 highest-risk employees based on the composite risk score, and are these employees plausibly concentrated in high-incident departments like Paint Shop?
criterion: The top-10 highest-risk employees should be disproportionately drawn from departments with the most incidents and compliance gaps: Paint Shop (14 total incidents, 7 OSHA recordable, 8 overdue/failed/incomplete OSHA records), Warehouse (10 overdue/failed/incomplete), and Assembly Line B (10 overdue/failed/incomplete).

Specific high-risk employees such as EMP-1001 (Betty Sanchez, Maintenance — 1 Overdue + 1 Failed on OSHA courses, involved in 1 training-related FIRE-101 incident) and Paint Shop/Warehouse/Assembly Line B employees with clustered compliance failures should be identified.
The response must highlight these top-10 employees specifically in the Compliance Matrix and explain why they rank highest based on the composite risk score methodology.
